what_it_does: Graph neural networks — AI models that reason about relationships in data, like social networks or molecules — are usually run on conventional chips that do a lot of software-managed computation. A different class of hardware called Electronic Dynamical Systems uses physical properties of electrical circuits (the way currents naturally settle into low-energy states, similar to how a ball rolls into a valley) to solve graph problems orders of magnitude faster with far less power. The problem is that these devices cannot update their own learned parameters and are limited to simple, linear relationships between connected nodes. DS-TPU adds two innovations: it feeds back a small electrical signal derived from the circuit's prediction error as a native learning signal, so the hardware can refine its parameters on the fly without sending work to a separate conventional processor; and it expresses richer, nonlinear relationships between nodes using a mathematical tool called Chebyshev polynomial expansions, which can be implemented in analog circuits. The result is a chip that can both run and continuously update a graph model, evaluated at five watts on six real-world graph learning tasks.
